overview: This file documents two connected aspects of U.S.–Japanese maritime administration between 1934 and 1938. The first group records successive appointments and removals of Japanese Bureau of Communications officials authorized to inspect ships and grant Panama Canal tonnage certificates. The second concerns Japan’s Ship Safety Law, its application to foreign vessels, and possible inspection fees: after the Department of Commerce raised the prospect of imposing reciprocal charges on Japanese vessels, the Embassy established that Japan did not charge American vessels for the limited inspections applicable to ships carrying recognized international safety and load-line certificates. The bundle includes diplomatic despatches, translated Foreign Ministry notes, State Department transmittals and instructions, cross-reference sheets, an internal drafting memorandum, and the translated text of the relevant Japanese ordinance.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1046 on the appointment of Akikata Mito
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Akikata Mito’s appointment as a Japanese ship inspector authorized to issue Panama Canal tonnage certificates.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Foreign Office notification that Department of Communications expert Akikata Mito was appointed ship inspector effective October 26, 1934. He encloses a translated Japanese note requesting that the appointment be communicated to the U.S. government.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office note on Akikata Mito’s appointment
subfiles.from: Kōki Hirota, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Officially notifies Grew of Akikata Mito’s appointment and asks him to inform the U.S. government.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Ministry states that Mito was appointed on October 26 and authorized under the regulations governing Panama Canal tonnage certificates. Hirota asks Grew to bring the information to his government’s attention.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the Mito appointment
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Chief of Office of the Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy’s report of Akikata Mito’s appointment for consideration and action.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends the Panama Canal a copy of Tokyo despatch No. 1046 and its enclosure. It identifies Mito as a Japanese Department of Communications expert empowered to issue tonnage certificates under Panama Canal rules.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1616 on the appointment of Toshio Teruki
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Toshio Teruki’s appointment as a ship inspector authorized to grant Panama Canal tonnage certificates.
subfiles.summary: Grew conveys the Japanese government’s request that Washington be informed of Teruki’s appointment. A translation of the supporting Foreign Ministry note is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office note on Toshio Teruki’s appointment
subfiles.from: Kōki Hirota, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Notifies the Embassy that Toshio Teruki was appointed a Panama Canal ship inspector on December 12, 1935.
subfiles.summary: Hirota reports that the Department of Communications appointed Bureau of Communications expert Toshio Teruki as a ship inspector. He asks Grew to communicate the appointment to the American government.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the Teruki appointment
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Chief of Office of the Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Forwards the report of Toshio Teruki’s appointment to the Panama Canal office.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses Tokyo despatch No. 1616 for information and any appropriate action. The covering text identifies Teruki’s authority to grant Panama Canal tonnage certificates.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2495 on changes among Japanese ship inspectors
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Kumaichi Shono’s appointment and the removal of Tsuneto To, Mikio Okubo, and Kiyosaburo Umeda as Panama Canal ship inspectors.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that Shono was appointed under the Panama Canal tonnage-certificate regulations effective June 11, 1937. Three other Bureau of Communications officials were simultaneously relieved, and a translated Japanese note is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office note on Shono and the relieved inspectors
subfiles.from: Kōki Hirota, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Officially communicates the appointment of Kumaichi Shono and the relief of three existing ship inspectors.
subfiles.summary: The note reports Shono’s appointment on June 11 under the regulations for Panama Canal tonnage certificates. It also identifies Tsuneto To, Mikio Okubo, and Kiyosaburo Umeda as the officials relieved and asks that Washington be informed.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the Shono appointment
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Chief of Office of the Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy’s report concerning Shono and the three relieved inspectors.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends Tokyo despatch No. 2495 to the Panama Canal. Its covering memorandum describes Shono as succeeding To, Okubo, and Umeda.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 1535 on Japanese inspection laws
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to file 195.4/272 for Arthur F. Tower’s August 31, 1937 despatch on Japanese ship-inspection laws and fees.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records the filing location of Tokyo despatch No. 1535. It describes the document as enclosing copies of Japanese inspection laws with a short commentary on the fees imposed under them.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1535 on Japanese ship-inspection laws and fees
subfiles.from: Arthur F. Tower, American Consul
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers a Commerce Department inquiry about Japanese vessel-inspection law, treatment of American ships, and applicable fees.
subfiles.summary: Tower encloses English translations of Japan’s Ship Safety Law and its enforcement regulations. He explains that foreign vessels possessing recognized safety and load-line certificates normally need not undergo inspection in Japan; vessels lacking them may be subjected to Japanese inspection requirements. Only one foreign vessel, a Chinese-registered ship without the required certificates and with an owner considered unreliable, had reportedly been inspected, and any foreign inspection would carry the same fees as an inspection of a Japanese vessel.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2577 on the appointment of Hidesaku Moriwaki
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Hidesaku Moriwaki’s appointment as an additional Panama Canal ship inspector.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Moriwaki was appointed effective August 18, 1937. He emphasizes that this appointment supplements rather than replaces Kumaichi Shono’s appointment.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office note on Moriwaki’s appointment
subfiles.from: Kōki Hirota, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Notifies the Embassy of Moriwaki’s appointment under the Panama Canal tonnage-certificate regulations.
subfiles.summary: Hirota reports receipt of a Department of Communications notice concerning Moriwaki’s appointment on August 18. He asks Grew to inform the American government.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the Moriwaki appointment
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Chief of Office of the Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Forwards notice that Moriwaki had been appointed in addition to Kumaichi Shono.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses Tokyo despatch No. 2577 for the Panama Canal’s consideration. It notes that Moriwaki’s appointment was supplementary to Shono’s previously reported appointment.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2610 on Junji Gohei and Shingo Nakano
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Junji Gohei’s appointment as ship inspector and Shingo Nakano’s relief from that office.
subfiles.summary: Grew states that Gohei was appointed under the Panama Canal tonnage-certificate regulations effective September 11, 1937. Nakano was relieved of duty, and the translated Foreign Ministry notice is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office note on Gohei and Nakano
subfiles.from: Kōki Hirota, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Officially reports Gohei’s appointment and Nakano’s removal as ship inspector.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies both men as Bureau of Communications experts and dates the personnel change to September 11. Hirota asks Grew to communicate the information to the U.S. government.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the Gohei appointment
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Chief of Office of the Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Forwards the report that Gohei replaced Nakano as a Panama Canal ship inspector.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses Tokyo despatch No. 2610. The memorandum summarizes Gohei’s appointment as a succession to Nakano, who had been relieved.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 24 on Japanese inspection fees
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to file 195.4/278 for a September 30, 1937 Tokyo despatch providing further information on Japanese inspection laws and fees.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Cameron as the originating officer and describes the referenced document as Despatch No. 24. It indicates that the despatch enclosed additional information about Japanese ship-inspection law and charges.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on identifying the Japanese fee tables
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Recommends clarifying that page references to fee tables are to the Mercantile Marine Bureau’s English translation of the Japanese ordinance.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum observes that the Tokyo Embassy normally works from original Japanese legal texts. It recommends adding language to the draft instruction that precisely identifies the English translation in which pages 75–79 appear.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department request for reciprocal exemption from inspection fees
subfiles.from: J. M. Johnson, Assistant Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests negotiations to exempt American and Japanese vessels reciprocally from ship-inspection fees.
subfiles.summary: Johnson warns that American vessels might be assessed fees under Japanese inspection law and asks the State Department to seek a reciprocal exemption. If negotiations fail, Commerce intends to impose equivalent fees on Japanese vessels at American ports under its statutory authority.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1401 on negotiating inspection-fee reciprocity
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State, signed by Hugh R. Wilson
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to determine whether Japan charges American vessels inspection fees and, if so, seek a reciprocal waiver.
subfiles.summary: The instruction reviews Japanese fee provisions and explains that Japanese ships receive limited certificate and safety inspections in the United States without charge. It quotes the U.S. statute requiring collection from foreign passenger steamers of the same fees their governments impose on American merchant ships. Grew is told to report whether Japan actually collects the listed fees and, if it does, propose a bilateral arrangement discontinuing them reciprocally. The December 22 date is confirmed by the later acknowledgment, although the OCR of the opening page reads December 12.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 54 on omitted inspection-law enclosures
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to file 195.4/286 for a Tokyo despatch concerning previously omitted enclosures on Japanese inspection laws and fees.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Cameron and an October 25, 1937 despatch numbered 54. It says that enclosures omitted from an August despatch were subsequently transmitted with a September 30 despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2803 on Japanese ship-inspection policy
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports that Japan charges no fees for the inspections of American vessels provided for under its foreign-vessel regulations.
subfiles.summary: Grew acknowledges Instruction No. 1401 and reports that the matter was raised informally with the Foreign Office. The written reply states that American vessels are not charged for the pertinent inspections. He encloses the Foreign Office communication and a revised translation of Ordinance No. 5 to replace the earlier version; the March 3 date is corroborated by the enclosures and final transmittal despite an OCR reading of March 8 on the first page.

subfiles.title: Mitani note explaining inspections of foreign vessels
subfiles.from: Takanobu Mitani, Director of the Bureau of Treaties
subfiles.to: Joseph F. McGurk, First Secretary, American Embassy
subfiles.about: Explains how Japan applies its safety and load-line inspection rules to foreign ships and confirms that qualifying inspections are free.
subfiles.summary: Mitani responds to McGurk’s January 19 inquiry after consulting the Ministry of Communications. Ships of treaty powers carrying recognized safety, wireless, exemption, or load-line certificates may have their documents examined and, if necessary, undergo limited verification without charge. Vessels outside these categories may be inspected like Japanese vessels and charged a fee, but Mitani states that this provision had never been applied.

subfiles.title: Revised Ordinance No. 5 on application of the Ship Safety Law to foreign vessels
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of Communications
subfiles.about: Sets out the Japanese rules governing safety inspections, certificates, load lines, tonnage measurement, and transitional exemptions for foreign vessels.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance specifies which Ship Safety Law provisions apply to foreign vessels and establishes limited inspection procedures for ships carrying internationally recognized certificates. It authorizes fuller inspection of vessels outside the treaty and certificate categories and regulates the calculation of foreign ships’ loading capacity. Supplementary provisions establish commencement and transitional periods for construction, equipment, load-line, and wireless requirements. The text was originally issued on February 1, 1934 and revised by Ordinance No. 26 in September 1935.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of Despatch No. 2803 to Commerce
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State
subfiles.to: The Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew’s confirmation that Japan does not charge American ships for the relevant inspections.
subfiles.summary: The State Department replies to Assistant Secretary Johnson’s October 27, 1937 letter by enclosing Despatch No. 2803 and its enclosures. The covering memorandum highlights the conclusion that no fees are charged to American ships for inspections conducted under Japanese law.

interest: The file is especially useful because it joins routine administrative notices about named Japanese ship inspectors to a substantive episode of maritime diplomacy. It shows how an apparent statutory basis for fees prompted the United States to contemplate retaliatory charges, only for inquiry in Tokyo to establish that recognized American certificates were examined without fees and that Japan’s fee-bearing residual provision had never been used. The translated ordinance and Mitani’s detailed explanation provide unusually concrete evidence about early port-state control, international recognition of safety, load-line, and wireless certificates, and the practical implementation of the interwar maritime conventions. The cross-reference sheets also reveal how related material was dispersed across the State Department decimal filing system.
